title: Mean-payoff games in polynomial time
formal:
Is the exact mean-payoff winner language \(\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\) defined below in deterministic polynomial time?

A valid instance is a finite directed graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(V=[n]\), \(n\ge1\), at least one outgoing edge at every vertex, a partition \(V=V_{\mathrm{Max}}\sqcup V_{\mathrm{Min}}\), an integer weight function \(w:E\to\mathbb Z\), and a start vertex \(s\in V\). Its encoding is in \(\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\) exactly when
\[\exists\sigma\in\Sigma_{\mathrm{Max}}\ \forall\tau\in\Sigma_{\mathrm{Min}},\qquad
\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac1T\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}w(v_t,v_{t+1})\ge0,\]
where \(v_0=s\) and the unique infinite play \((v_t)_{t\ge0}\) follows the two strategies. Weights have the binary encoding specified below, and equality zero counts as winning for Max. Give a complete Lean proof of \(\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\in\mathrm P\) or of \(\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\notin\mathrm P\).
definitions:
The edge set is a subset of \(V\times V\); self-loops are allowed and duplicate edges are not listed. Every listed edge has one arbitrary integer weight, possibly negative or zero. Either ownership set may be empty, and edges may connect vertices of the same owner. There are no chance vertices, additional agents, hidden information, simultaneous moves, fairness constraints, or extra payoff coordinates. Every vertex has a successor, so no finite-play convention is needed.

A finite history from \(s\) is a nonempty vertex sequence \(h=(s=v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_t)\) following edges of \(E\). A strategy of Max assigns to every such history ending in \(V_{\mathrm{Max}}\) a successor \(v\) with \((v_t,v)\in E\); define a strategy of Min analogously. The sets of these total deterministic history-dependent functions are \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{Max}}\) and \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{Min}}\). Neither player sees future choices. A strategy may depend on the complete known instance and entire finite history; the problem statement places no memory or computability restriction on strategies. For any pair, the play is uniquely determined by recursion. A positional strategy means that the selected successor depends only on the current vertex; positional optimality is an established theorem, not an additional promise on the instance.

For \(T\ge1\), set \(a_T=T^{-1}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}w(v_t,v_{t+1})\). The lower limit means
\[\liminf_{T\to\infty}a_T=\sup_{N\ge1}\inf_{T\ge N}a_T.\]
It is a finite real number because \(|a_T|\le W\), where \(W=\max(1,\max_{e\in E}|w(e)|)\). The average need not converge for arbitrary history-dependent play. A negative finite prefix is allowed: this objective imposes no lower bound on the running cumulative sum and no prescribed initial energy budget. The payoff is not a discounted sum or a finite-window average.

For a concrete binary encoding, let \(b(u)\) be the binary expansion of a nonnegative integer \(u\), without leading zeros and with \(b(0)=0\). Define \(B(u)=1^{|b(u)|}0b(u)\). Encode an integer \(z\) by \(B(\zeta(z))\), where \(\zeta(z)=2z\) for \(z\ge0\) and \(\zeta(z)=-2z-1\) for \(z<0\). This is a signed binary representation with a uniquely recoverable sign and magnitude; it is not unary in \(|z|\).

The input is \(B(n)B(m)B(s)\), followed by the \(n\) ownership bits in vertex order, and then \(m=|E|\) triples \(B(u)B(v)B(\zeta(w(u,v)))\), listing edges in increasing lexicographic endpoint order. Ownership bit one denotes Max and zero denotes Min. The complete string must satisfy the stated graph and encoding conditions, with no trailing bits. All other binary strings are rejected and are outside \(\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\). Let \(L\) denote the complete input length. Input validation and the translation to ordinary explicit adjacency-list signed-binary representations are polynomial-time operations; these representation conventions do not impose a graph or weight promise.

Membership in \(\mathrm P\) means that there are a finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) such that for every binary string \(x\), \(A(x)\) halts within \(C(|x|+1)^d\) bit steps, outputting one exactly when \(x\in\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}\). The same program and constants must work for every size, graph, weight assignment and start vertex. Input reading, validation, arithmetic, storage access and output all count. There is no advice, randomization, game-solving oracle or unit-cost operation on arbitrarily large integers. The polynomial may depend on the fixed program but not on \(n,m,W\) or the instance. The output is only the exact winner bit; the task does not require printing an infinite strategy or play.

There is no bound on \(W\) in terms of \(n\) or \(m\). Its contribution to the input is logarithmic, so a bound polynomial in \(n,m,W\) is pseudopolynomial and need not be polynomial in \(L\). A rational threshold \(a/b\), with binary integers \(a\) and \(b>0\), gives an equivalent decision model: the weights \(bw(e)-a\) have polynomial encoding length and their nonnegative mean threshold expresses the original threshold. Thus fixing the threshold to zero retains the binary-weight complexity question.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of either
\[\exists A\ \exists C,d\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall x\in\{0,1\}^{*},\quad
 A(x)\text{ halts within }C(|x|+1)^d\text{ steps and outputs }\mathbf1_{\mathrm{MPG}_{\ge0}}(x),\]
or its logical negation, with the machine and language definitions above. A positive proof must establish the exact game semantics, correctness on every valid instance, rejection of invalid encodings, and the full polynomial bit bound. A negative proof must rule out every deterministic polynomial-time decider, rather than only a particular local-improvement rule, representation, certificate family or algorithmic framework.

A pseudopolynomial bound, a polynomial bound only after random perturbations, a randomized expected-time guarantee, or an algorithm for a restricted graph or weight family does not answer the full question. A polynomial number of arithmetic operations alone is insufficient if intermediate integers require superpolynomial bit length. A strongly polynomial algorithm with polynomially bounded bit representations would suffice but is more than required. There is no approximation tolerance or unproved complexity hypothesis in the target.
why: Mean-payoff games model sustainable long-run rewards when an adversary controls part of a finite system. Their exact winner problem has short certificates for both answers, yet its unrestricted polynomial bit complexity remains an important question in quantitative verification and graph-game theory.

importance.reason: A canonical NP∩coNP problem central to quantitative synthesis and long-run control; resolving the binary-weight complexity gap would have consequences across several equivalent algebraic and game formulations.

progress.text: Zwick–Paterson study positional certificates, pseudopolynomial algorithms and the reduction to simple stochastic games.
Brim and coauthors give the \(O(nmW)\) pseudopolynomial threshold and strategy-synthesis bound in Theorem 8.
MFCS publishes upper and lower bounds for the universal-graph value-iteration framework; the lower bounds retain that framework restriction.
ICALP publishes smoothed guarantees on ergodic graphs, with independent reward perturbations. The published hypotheses are retained.
Maat’s preprint gives a nondegenerate strategy-improvement/simplex correspondence and records the large coefficient obstruction to polynomial bit complexity.
Ohlmann introduces a deterministic symmetric recursive solver, leaving its intended improved complexity bound open.
The set-defined graph-class preprint gives new reductions and explicitly retains the binary-weight polynomial-time question.

status_note: Source-open evidence checked on 15 September 2026. The July 2026 primary source explicitly leaves polynomial complexity in the binary weight length open; the March 2026 recursive solver also leaves its improved runtime analysis open. The inspected pseudopolynomial, universal-graph, ergodic smoothed-analysis, simplex-correspondence and restricted-signature results do not establish membership in P or exclusion from P for the exact language here. Bounded searches found no full matching resolution claim. The new smoothed-algorithm author-page title was not assigned a theorem beyond the inspected evidence. This review checks statement and source scope, not every cited proof or an exhaustive certification of present openness.

context_blocks.text: A finite initial loss disappears from a long-run average. For example, an eventual repetition of weights −5 and +7 has mean payoff one after any fixed finite prefix. Requiring every partial sum to stay nonnegative is a different objective. A play of weight zero forever is winning here because the threshold is nonnegative, not strictly positive.

Optimal positional strategies exist for both players. With both such strategies fixed, a finite graph produces an eventually repeated cycle, whose average determines the payoff. The resulting certificates place the winner language in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\): yes and no instances each have polynomial-length certificates checkable in polynomial time. This does not provide a polynomial-time way to find them. Zwick and Paterson give the classical complexity analysis and a polynomial reduction to simple stochastic games, which add random transitions.

Brim and coauthors' Theorem 8 gives \(O(nmW)\) arithmetic-operation bounds for threshold decision and winning-strategy synthesis, where \(n=|V|\) and \(m=|E|\). A weight of magnitude \(2^b\) requires only \(b+1\) magnitude bits. Thus this dependence can be exponential in the encoding length even before charging for arithmetic. Their theorem is pseudopolynomial; it is not a uniform polynomial bit bound for arbitrary weights.

Fijalkow, Gawrychowski and Ohlmann establish size bounds for universal graphs, auxiliary weighted graphs that represent all bounded-size graphs satisfying the mean-payoff objective through weight-preserving maps. Their lower bounds constrain the resulting family of value-iteration algorithms. They do not exclude algorithms outside that framework, so they do not prove that the winner language is outside P.

The published ICALP 2024 theorem of Loff and Skomra assumes an ergodic game graph and independent random perturbations of rewards. Ergodic means that for every reward assignment the game value is independent of the starting vertex; ordinary strong connectivity does not imply this property. For example, Theorem 1 gives time polynomial in \(n\) and the inverse perturbation scale for normalized rewards perturbed by independent Gaussians, with high probability over those perturbations. Both the input restriction and probabilistic guarantee remain part of the theorem.

Maat’s September 2025 preprint identifies strategy improvement with simplex runs for a nondegenerate longest-shortest-path game formulation. Nondegeneracy excludes certain zero cycles and equal-weight competing paths. Section 5 explicitly warns that the constructed linear-program coefficients can have doubly exponential magnitudes, so writing them may require exponentially many bits. The existence of this linear program and its correspondence between iterations therefore do not supply a polynomial-bit-time solver.

Ohlmann’s March 2026 preprint gives a new deterministic recursive algorithm and a correctness argument. Its introduction and Section 7 explicitly leave a useful running-time analysis, including the hoped-for subexponential bound, unresolved. It does not claim a polynomial-time solution. Its presentation uses limsup and positional strategies; positional determinacy of these finite games preserves the game value, while the present definition retains its explicit liminf objective for arbitrary histories.

Adenwalla and coauthors’ July 2026 preprint relates mean-payoff games to tropical inequalities and graph classes defined by equality patterns among vertex labels. Tropical linear expressions replace ordinary addition and multiplication by maximum and addition. Section 7 gives a reduction using compact encodings of path clauses and functional constraints; it does not assume that an exponentially long clause is written out. This is a connection between decision problems, while Section 3.7.2 explicitly leaves polynomial-time mean-payoff solving open.

sentences: Two players control different vertices of a finite integer-weighted graph and choose an infinite path from a specified start.
Max wins when the lower limit of the average weight is nonnegative against every history-dependent strategy of Min, including exact equality zero.
The question is whether the resulting binary-input winner language has one deterministic decider running in polynomial bit time on all inputs.
Positional certificates and pseudopolynomial algorithms are known, but large binary weights leave a gap to the required complexity.
Recent recursive, smoothed and linear-programming connections retain runtime, distributional or encoding limitations and do not settle the full target.

source_formulation.text: The classical polynomial-time question for mean-payoff games concerns the bit length of binary weights, not their numerical magnitude. The July 2026 source restates this distinction explicitly in Section 3.7.2. This card retains its deterministic single-start, zero-threshold liminf winner problem and adds a concrete encoding and total decision-language convention.
